sections.title: The Mitzva
sections.html:
The Torah commanded not to wear a garment made of wool and linen, as it is stated (Vayikra 19:19): "You shall keep My statutes: you shall not let your animals mate with a different kind; you shall not sow your field with kil'ayim; and a garment of kil'ayim, sha'atnez, shall not come upon you." And it is likewise stated (Devarim 22:11): "You shall not wear sha'atnez, wool and linen together."

Wool is what grows on the species called "sheep," whose males are called rams and whose females are called ewes. But what grows on other animals is not included in the prohibition, because it is not called simply "wool," but rather has a qualifying name. Therefore, there is no prohibition with "camel wool," "goat wool" (such as cashmere), "rabbit wool" (such as angora), and "alpaca wool." In practice, from ancient times until our day, most of the wool produced in the world is from sheep, because by their nature they grow abundant, high-quality wool, and they are easy for people to raise.

Flax is a plant with a single long stalk, and inside its stalk there are fibers from which strong threads can be made, and with special processing fine threads can be spun from them for weaving handsome white garments. The prohibition applies to linen and not to threads from other plants, such as hemp and cotton. In the past, the common garments were made of wool or linen, to the point that some hold that when the Torah says "garment" without specifying, it means a garment made of wool or linen (Menaḥot 39b).

The prohibition of sha'atnez is to wear a garment that contains wool and linen, but there is no prohibition against wearing two garments, one of wool and one of linen. Therefore it is permitted to wear woolen trousers and a linen shirt. Likewise it is permitted to wear a woolen robe and gird it with a linen belt, for as long as there is no connection by sewing or a permanent knot between the woolen garment and the linen garment, there is no prohibition (below, 6).

The prohibition is to wear garments that contain wool and linen, but there is no prohibition against making sha'atnez cloth in order to hang it on the wall for decoration, or so that it will serve as a parokhet (curtain) for the Holy Ark, or in order to make from it a cloth purse or a tent. Likewise, it is permitted to make shrouds for the dead from sha'atnez cloth, for the dead are exempt from the mitzvot. Likewise, it is permitted to manufacture a sha'atnez garment for gentiles, provided there is no concern that the garment will reach a Jew who will mistakenly wear it.

sections.title: The Prohibition of Wearing and of Placing Upon Oneself
sections.html:
Clothing is meant to protect a person from cold, heat or rain, and it is also meant for beauty, dignity and covering the body modestly. Any person who wears a sha'atnez garment for one of these purposes transgresses a prohibition, as it is stated (Devarim 22:11): "You shall not wear sha'atnez." Included in the prohibition are a shirt, trousers, a dress, a skirt, underwear, socks, hats, cloth shoes, gloves, a tie and decorative ribbons, and all other garments that people usually wear. Even when the hanging loop of the garment or the label attached to it is sha'atnez, the garment is forbidden to wear (SA YD 301:15).

One who places sha'atnez cloth upon himself in order to protect his body from cold or heat, or in order to cover his body modestly, even though he placed it upon himself not in the manner of wearing, transgresses a prohibition, as it is stated (Vayikra 19:19): "and a garment of kil'ayim, sha'atnez, shall not come upon you." Thus, anything from which one derives benefit in the way one benefits from a garment is forbidden. Therefore, it is forbidden to cover oneself with a sha'atnez blanket. Likewise, it is forbidden to use a sha'atnez towel, because one who dries his body or his hands is warmed by it. The Sages even forbade using tablecloths made of sha'atnez, lest one sometimes warm one's thighs a little with them (SA 301:9). Likewise, they forbade hanging a sha'atnez curtain, because people or children sometimes warm themselves with it; but it is permitted to hang it above a person's height, or when it is made of stiff cloth, since it is not possible to warm oneself with it (ibid. 11). It is forbidden to take hold of a hot pot or something frozen with a sha'atnez cloth, since one derives benefit from the cloth in a way similar to clothing, in that it protects his hand from the heat or the cold (ibid. 12).

But not in the manner of benefit from clothing, it is permitted to derive benefit from sha'atnez cloth. Therefore, it is permitted to use sha'atnez cloth for a tent or an umbrella.

Furthermore, according to many, it is permitted to wear a sha'atnez garment not for the purposes of clothing. For example, a Jew who needs to cross a border carrying in his bag gentiles' sha'atnez garments on which he must pay customs duty may wear them over his clothes while crossing the border, in order to be exempt from the duty, which is imposed only on garments in a bag, provided he does not intend to benefit from wearing them. Likewise, a clothing seller is permitted to wear garments in order to display them to buyers, provided he does not intend to benefit from them (Rosh, Ramban, Ran, Rema 301:6; Yam Shel Shlomo). And some are stringent and forbid wearing sha'atnez in order to be exempt from customs duty (Rambam, SA 301:5).1

sections.title: Spreading Beneath Oneself and Stiff Cloth
sections.html:
By Torah law it is permitted to sit or lie on sha'atnez cloth, and although one is warmed by it, the Torah prohibition applies only when the sha'atnez is above the person or at his side in the manner of a garment, and not beneath him, as it is stated (Vayikra 19:19): "and a garment of kil'ayim, sha'atnez, shall not come upon you." However, the Sages forbade sitting or lying on sha'atnez cloth, lest a thread rise from it and wrap around his flesh through some contact, or lest he mistakenly wrap himself in it. So that people would not err in this, the Sages further decreed that the prohibition against sitting or lying on sha'atnez cloth applies even if there were ten permitted cloths on top of it (Beitza 14b; SA 301:1).

But if the sha'atnez cloth is stiff, to the point that it cannot be used as a garment because of its stiffness, and it lies on a floor or a chair into which one does not sink, the Sages did not forbid sitting and lying on it, provided there is something separating between it and the body, so that if a thread comes out of the sha'atnez cloth it will not be able to wrap around his flesh (SA 301:1). Therefore, it is permitted to lie on a stiff sha'atnez carpet when another cloth is spread over it, and it is likewise permitted to sit on a chair over which sha'atnez cloth is stretched, when one's trousers or dress separate between the body and the chair. And although the sha'atnez cloth stretched over the chair is soft, as long as it is stretched over a chair with nails or glue, its law is like that of stiff cloth (Panim Me'irot 2:113).2

sections.title: What Is Sha'atnez
sections.html:
To make a garment of wool or linen, the raw wool or flax must undergo three stages that are alluded to in the word "sha'atnez," as explained in the Mishna (Kil'ayim 9:8): "Sha'atnez: something that is shu'a (smoothed), tavui (spun) and nuz (twisted together)." a) Shu'a – smoothing the wool or flax by combing. b) Tavui – creating a thread from the fibers of the wool and flax. c) Nuz – intertwining. The intertwining can be by weaving the linen and wool threads as warp and weft to make cloth, or by binding linen threads onto a woolen garment by way of tying or sewing.

As a matter of halakha, in four main ways the joining is forbidden: a) When the wool and flax were mixed at the raw stage, and while together they were smoothed, made into threads, and woven into cloth. b) When the wool was made into wool threads and the flax into linen threads, and they were woven into one cloth, for example where the linen threads are the warp and the wool threads are the weft. c) Woolen cloth was sewn or tied with linen threads, or vice versa. d) Woolen cloth and linen cloth were joined by sewing.

The common denominator of all these ways is that the wool and flax underwent the three stages of shu'a, tavui and nuz. But when the wool and flax did not undergo the three stages, as with felt cloths, which are made from raw wool or flax by compression without spinning and weaving, according to the overwhelming majority of the Rishonim joining them does not involve the Torah prohibition of sha'atnez. And some disagree and hold that even if the wool and flax underwent only the first stage of smoothing and combing and were made into felt, joining them involves a Torah prohibition (Rambam).3

sections.title: Threads Composed of Two Kinds
sections.html:
With a thread composed of sheep's wool and another kind such as cotton, we follow the majority: if the majority is cotton, we are not concerned about the fine wool fibers in it, and its law is that of a cotton thread, which may be joined to linen. Likewise, a thread composed of hemp and flax, if the majority is hemp, may be joined to wool. Not only that, but even if raw wool and raw flax became mixed, it is permitted to add another kind such as cotton that will exceed one of them and nullify it, and then the threads made from this mixture will be permissible; but if there was not another kind exceeding the wool or the flax, a garment woven from the threads produced from the mixture is forbidden by Torah law (Yerushalmi Kil'ayim 9:1; SA 299:1).

The wool and flax can be nullified in a majority at the stage when they are raw, but once they have been made into threads they have importance and are not nullified even in a thousand. For example, a cotton garment sewn with wool and linen threads twisted together – even if the cotton garment contains a thousand times their amount, the garment is forbidden by Torah law. Likewise, if a small wool thread became mixed into a large linen garment or vice versa, all of it is forbidden; and even if the location of the wool thread has been lost, as long as it has not been removed, the entire garment is forbidden (SA and Rema 299:1).4

sections.title: Joining Is Forbidden, Wearing Together Is Permitted
sections.html:
Whenever the wool and the linen have been joined to one another with a complete joining, the garment is forbidden by Torah law because of sha'atnez. For example, a skirt in which woolen cloth and linen cloth are sewn to one another, or a woolen coat that has a hanging loop or loops of linen, are forbidden by Torah law.

But if there is no joining between the wool and the linen, for example a cotton garment to one side of which woolen cloth was sewn, and to its other side linen cloth, since there is no joining between the wool and the linen, according to most poskim there is no prohibition. Likewise, when woolen cloth and linen cloth were placed inside a lining, since they were not joined to one another, it is permitted (Rash, Ramban, Rosh and Rashba). And according to the Rambam, whenever they are joined to a single garment, the entire garment is forbidden by Torah law. In practice, the custom is to be lenient, and the meticulous are stringent (Rema 300:5).5

The prohibition of sha'atnez applies when the wool and the linen are joined, but when they are not joined, there is no prohibition against wearing them together. Therefore, it is permitted to wear a woolen shirt over a linen shirt and to put a belt around them; likewise it is permitted to gird linen trousers with a woolen belt; and likewise it is permitted to connect a woolen garment and a linen garment with buttons that open easily or with Velcro, because in all these cases there is no permanent joining between the woolen garment and the linen garment, but rather they are held together in a temporary manner (SA and Rema 300:3-4).6

Some say that one should not put on woolen socks over linen socks, for since it is not possible to remove the linen socks without first removing the woolen socks, they are considered joined with a strong joining (Rema 300:4). However, according to most poskim, since there is no permanent joining there, it is permitted, and this is the practice (SA 300:4, Levush, Shakh 8, Arukh Ha-shulḥan 24).

sections.title: Wool and Linen Garments in the Past and the Present
sections.html:
In the past, most garments were produced from wool or linen. What is special about woolen garments is that they insulate and preserve body heat in winter. In addition, they tend to absorb less dirt and rain tends to slide off them, and since they also retain warmth, coats are commonly made from them. Wool also takes dye easily and holds the color as part of the thread. Wool tends to return to its basic shape, so if it is creased it tends to straighten out. For these reasons woolen garments stay like new for a relatively long time.

Linen cloths were considered pleasant, high-quality cloths, because linen threads are strong, and when fine threads are spun from them, especially handsome white garments can be woven from them, while the unevenness in the thickness of the linen thread, which results from its natural growth, gives linen garments a beautiful and interesting appearance. So much so that the Sages said that it is a mitzva for men in the Land of Israel to gladden their wives on the festival with a gift of pressed linen garments, which were especially beloved to them (Pesaḥim 109a). What characterizes linen cloth is that it is light and does not insulate, and therefore it is suitable for making light summer garments through which the wind blows and cools those who wear them. Their drawback is that they crease a great deal and absorb dirt, and they are relatively difficult to clean. Therefore, when a substitute for linen was found, its status declined greatly.

Cotton garments, whose production began to be widespread several hundred years ago, are the natural substitute for linen garments. Cotton garments are indeed a little warmer than linen garments, but they are preferable to them, because it is easier to grow cotton and produce threads from it, and cotton garments crease less and are easier to wash. Thus we have reached a situation in which today the world produces eighty times more cotton than linen, with most of the linen intended for the production of strong threads and other purposes that are not clothing. Since it is possible to produce thick cotton garments for winter, cotton has to a large extent replaced wool as well. The quantity of cotton produced in the world today is twenty-five times that of wool. There are additional threads from kinds of plants and animals that also contribute to a certain reduction in the percentage of wool and linen in the clothing industry.

About three generations ago a way was found to produce from petroleum by-products synthetic products such as plastic, nylon, and artificial threads such as polyester and acrylic, from which cloth can be made. At first, synthetic garments were impermeable and did not insulate, and those who wore them suffered from sweat and cold, and only their low price allowed them to compete with natural garments. But the process of improving them continued, and they became more breathable and insulating, and since they are also cheaper and easy to clean and iron, they became extremely widespread. In recent years they have been further improved, until we have reached a situation in which today (5778 [2018]) more than 70% of all threads produced in the world are synthetic (ten years ago they were 60%). In practice, the share of wool and linen in the entire clothing industry has fallen to only one percent, and apparently their share will continue to fall.7

So it turns out that in practice only rarely can one find luxury shirts and suits made of linen. More common is the use of linen threads and cloths, which thanks to their strength are good for tying objects and for weaving thick cloths, and sometimes linen cloths are used to reinforce various parts of coats and suits, for example to reinforce the collar of the suit, and to reinforce the places to which buttons and loops are sewn.

For the reasons mentioned, woolen garments have also decreased, but thanks to their warming quality and their tendency not to absorb rain and dirt, people who prefer a natural, breathable material prefer woolen sweaters, and thanks to their luxurious appearance, many prefer woolen suits and coats.

sections.title: Guarding Against Sha'atnez in Practice
sections.html:
In the overwhelming majority of the garments bought today there is no concern of sha'atnez, because they are made of synthetic materials or of cotton. Therefore, whenever it is written on the garment that it is made mainly of synthetic materials, or of cotton, or of other materials that are not wool or linen, one need not be concerned that it may contain sha'atnez. Indeed, in rare cases a decoration of wool or linen may be attached to garments, or the garment may be sewn with linen threads, and in extremely rare cases it may happen that both linen threads and a woolen decoration are attached to the garment. But since this is a very remote concern, one need not be concerned about it. Moreover, according to most poskim, as long as there is no joining between the wool and the linen, there is no prohibition (above, 6). Therefore, one should read the label on the garment, and if it does not say that it is made of wool or linen, one need not be concerned about sha'atnez.

Also with woolen garments or linen garments, it suffices for the buyer to look at the garment's label: if it says that it is made of wool or of linen with additional kinds, without a mixture of wool and linen, there is no need to check it. Indeed, sometimes the label is not accurate, either because if it contains linen or wool in an amount of one or two percent there is no obligation to state it, or because occasionally a mistake is made and the label of another garment is attached to the garment. But in practice, as long as it is not written on the label that the garment contains wool and linen, the likelihood that it contains sha'atnez is far lower than a "mi'ut ha-matzui" (a common minority), and therefore there is no need to check it. Also with ordinary woolen suits and coats, the likelihood that linen was mixed in is so remote that one need not be concerned about it.

The concern of sha'atnez may exist with luxury woolen suits and coats, whose price is very high, which are occasionally hand-tailored with linen threads. And sometimes the collar and the areas around the buttons are reinforced with strong linen cloths, and sometimes a lining of linen cloth is inserted in the shoulders and the front. Therefore, one who buys a very expensive woolen suit or coat, since in a "common minority" of them linen is mixed in, is obligated to check them. Likewise, it is proper for one who buys a linen suit to check it, since there is a certain concern that wool was placed in its collar.

The place for checking is a sha'atnez testing laboratory, where a microscope is used, by means of which one can see the fibers of which the thread is made; and since each thread has a form of its own, one who knows the forms of the threads can distinguish between wool and linen, and between them and threads of other types. As a rule, the position of the testers in the laboratories tends to take into account the minority stringent opinions, both regarding the laws of sha'atnez and regarding the obligation to check.

Everything we have learned so far concerns buyers, but greater responsibility rests on the owners of clothing stores, and they must beware of every doubt, so as not to cause the public to stumble in the prohibition of sha'atnez. Whenever they receive woolen or linen garments about which, from their experience, there is some concern, even if it is less than a "common minority," they should send a sample of the garments for testing, and if the sample comes out clean, they need not test the rest of the garments of the same series. And when, according to their experience, there is no concern with them, there is no need to send them for testing. On the other hand, when the concern is great, such as with expensive suits and coats, they should send all of them for testing.

It is proper for buyers to prefer buying woolen or linen garments from God-fearing sellers who take care not to cause buyers to stumble in the prohibition of sha'atnez. However, if they bought in an ordinary store, they are obligated to check only especially expensive woolen suits and coats, and linen suits.8

sections.title: One Who Finds Kil'ayim in His Garment
sections.html:
In the past, sha'atnez was evident, since most threads and cloths were of wool or linen, and many people knew how to distinguish between them. There were garments in which the sha'atnez was very evident, to the point that within the Jewish community it was clear that any Jew who wore them was thereby defying the custom of Israel and publicly desecrating the name of Heaven. And there were garments that most Jews knew were sha'atnez, but not everyone noticed it, and there were garments in which only experts could detect the sha'atnez. Thus a situation could arise in which a person bought a garment and wore it, and suddenly, while in the marketplace, it became clear to him that he was wearing sha'atnez forbidden by Torah law. Then the halakha is that he must take off the garment, even though he will remain naked in the middle of the street and be embarrassed, because "there is no wisdom, no understanding and no counsel against God"; wherever there is a desecration of God's name, honor is not accorded even to a rabbi (Berakhot 19a; SA 303:1).

And if he did not remove it because of embarrassment, some say that by virtue of the mitzva of rebuke and the mutual responsibility of all Israel for one another, it is a mitzva for his fellow to tear the garment off him (Rambam and SA 303:1). This is provided that the fellow agrees that this is the halakha, only it is difficult for him to fulfill it, and it is reasonable that in the end he will be grateful to his fellow for tearing the garment off him and saving him from the prohibition. But if the one wearing sha'atnez has cast off the yoke of the mitzvot, since tearing the garment will not bring him closer to Torah and mitzvot, one should not tear the garment off him. And according to many, even in a situation where the fellow in principle agrees with the halakha, one should rebuke him but not tear his garment (Rosh, Rashba, Ra'ah, Terumat Ha-deshen).

If a person sees that his fellow has inadvertently put on a sha'atnez garment, and removing it would cause him great embarrassment, according to many he should not point this out to him, so that he will not have to remove the garment and be embarrassed; rather, he should call him to his home and there tell him that he is wearing sha'atnez (Rosh, Terumat Ha-deshen and Rema). And some say that he should inform him immediately, so that he will remove the garment as soon as possible (Rambam and Radbaz).9

sections.title: Kil'ayim in the Priestly Garments and in Tzitzit
sections.html:
Together with the prohibition of sha'atnez, the Torah commanded two mitzvot relating to clothing in which there is to be sha'atnez in the garment: in the priestly garments and in tzitzit.

The kohanim must wear four garments while performing their service: a tunic, trousers and a turban – all three were of white linen cloth; the fourth garment was a sash into which wool and linen threads were interwoven, for the sash was twisted from four threads, one white of linen, and the three others of dyed wool, one in tekhelet (sky-blue), the second in argaman (purple), and the third in tola'at shani (crimson), for every thread that the Torah requires to be dyed must be of wool, since wool absorbs the dye well. The kohen gadol had four more garments: a robe, an efod, a breastplate (ḥoshen) and a headplate (tzitz), and in two of them, the breastplate and the efod, it is a mitzva to combine wool and linen. The permission for the kohanim to wear sha'atnez is during the time of their service in the Temple, but when they left the Temple they had to take off the priestly garments, so as not to transgress the prohibition of sha'atnez.10

Regarding sha'atnez and tzitzit it is stated (Devarim 22:11-12): "You shall not wear sha'atnez, wool and linen together. You shall make for yourself twisted cords (tzitzit) on the four corners of your garment with which you cover yourself." The Sages learned from the juxtaposition of the verses that despite the prohibition of sha'atnez, sha'atnez is permitted in tzitzit. For it is a mitzva that the cord of tzitzit placed on the corners of the tallit be composed of white threads and tekhelet threads, and the threads dyed with tekhelet were of wool; it follows that if the garment is made of linen, the Torah commanded that there be sha'atnez in it. From this we learn a general rule, that whenever there is a clash between a positive mitzva and a negative mitzva, the positive mitzva prevails and the negative mitzva is set aside before it (Yevamot 4a-b). However, in practice, the Sages decreed not to place woolen tekhelet threads on a linen garment, but rather to suffice with white tzitzit threads alone, lest one wear the garment at night, which is a time when one is exempt from tzitzit, and transgress the prohibition of sha'atnez (Menaḥot 40a-b, Shabbat 25b; Rambam, Hilkhot Tzitzit 3:6-7).11

sections.title: The Reasons for the Mitzva
sections.html:
The prohibitions of kil'ayim and sha'atnez are Divine statutes whose essence human reason cannot comprehend; nevertheless, the sages of the generations offered various reasons for the mitzva, the central one being that the Divine law is that wool and linen have different properties, and each kind has its own purpose, and God commanded that we give each kind its own distinct place and not mix them (Ramban, Vayikra 19:19).

Wool and linen are the two main kinds from which garments were made, and they are kinds that are different and utterly opposed. Wool is produced from the animal kingdom and alludes to the attribute of ḥesed (kindness); linen is produced from the plant kingdom and alludes to the attribute of din (strict judgment); and joining them is a complex and difficult matter. Therefore the Torah commanded joining them within the framework of a mitzva, in the priestly garments and in tzitzit, so that in this way their joining will be in holiness, and each force will be actualized in the proper way, adding blessing and life. Furthermore, since it is a mitzva to mix wool and linen in the priestly garments and in tzitzit, it is not proper for a person to use this special mixture for mundane matters, for it is intended for holiness alone (Da'at Zekenim, Devarim 22:11; Ḥizkuni, Vayikra 19:19; Metzudat David of the Radbaz 235; Likutei Halakhot, Kil'ei Begadim 1).

It was further said that only within the framework of a mitzva can the opposing forces be actualized properly, but not for the sake of a mitzva, their mixing causes the imprisonment of the good forces and prevents them from being actualized (Zohar III 86b). For within the framework of a mitzva, ḥesed and din find proper expression, but when they are mixed together, the evil inclination uses them for evil (Mikhtav Me-Eliyahu vol. 4, p. 176). For example, when a person needs to give tzedaka, it is convenient for the evil inclination to wrap itself in the attribute of din and argue that this poor person does not deserve tzedaka. And on the other hand, when one needs to stand up for the truth and save a person from the hand of a wicked man who is oppressing him, it is convenient for the evil inclination to wrap itself in the attribute of ḥesed and find merit in the wicked man, in order to be exempt from the obligation to rise to the aid of the oppressed.

One can say that through the separation between the two kinds that by their nature were the most suitable for making garments, and their joining within the framework of a mitzva, man learned to produce and create additional threads in which the human element that blends the natural properties is more prominent, and therefore blending them is easy and simple, and consequently involves neither prohibition nor mitzva.12
